title: DiWALI: Diffusion Policy Learning in World Models via Latent Action Inference from Human and Robot Play
summary: Learning robot manipulation is constrained by the availability of action-labeled robot data, for both imitation and world models. Humans can demonstrate skills in seconds, but their demonstrations lack the required robot actions.

extra.full_text: Learning robot manipulation is constrained by the availability of action-labeled robot data, for both imitation and world models. Humans can demonstrate skills in seconds, but their demonstrations lack the required robot actions. We introduce DiWALI, a framework that learns and improves diffusion policies within a world model trained on human and robot play. DiWALI infers latent actions from consecutive frames using an inverse dynamics model, enabling world model training without action labels, and grounds them in robot commands through a decoder trained separately on robot play. Skill policies are trained over latent actions from action-free human demonstrations and improved with reinforcement learning in imagination. On the CALVIN benchmark, DiWALI policies trained solely from human demonstrations substantially outperform baselines trained with robot demonstrations. Incorporating human play into the world model training also yields stronger policies after fine-tuning than using the same amount of robot play alone. Experiments on a physical robot show that skills learned primarily from human demonstrations are further improved in imagination with a world model trained on human and robot play. Together, these results demonstrate that human experience can support both manipulation skill acquisition and subsequent policy improvement, reducing reliance on action-labeled robot data. Videos, dataset and code are available at https://diwali.cs.uni-freiburg.de.

title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations.

extra.comment: Apoorva Vashisth and Manav Kulshrestha contributed equally to this work. Prof. Zachary Kingston and Prof. Aniket Bera jointly advised this work
extra.full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

title: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place.

extra.comment: 17 pages, 13 figures, 17 tables (including supplementary material). Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/
extra.full_text: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.

title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
summary: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators.

extra.full_text: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

title: 3DTouch: A Tactile-aware VLA Model with 3D Geometric Relations for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, occlusion by the fingers and interacting objects obscures local geometry, preventing visual observations from fully capturing contact locations. Visually similar scenes may also differ subtly in the relative positions of interacting objects, leading to different contact states.

extra.full_text: In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, occlusion by the fingers and interacting objects obscures local geometry, preventing visual observations from fully capturing contact locations. Visually similar scenes may also differ subtly in the relative positions of interacting objects, leading to different contact states. We propose 3DTouch, a tactile-geometric conditioning approach for vision-language-action (VLA) models. 3DTouch constructs a shared 3D visuo-tactile representation by expressing RGB-D scene points and dense five-finger tactile measurements in the robot-base frame, preserving each taxel's spatial location and force vector. Hand-object and object-object relations derived from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces explicitly describe the relative arrangement of interacting entities. Together, these representations condition the VLA action expert on spatially localized contact forces and relative surface geometry, providing explicit cues for contact adjustment and object alignment. We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and by 20 percentage points over the strongest evaluated alternative. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with further gains from shared spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations.

title: GTI: Grounding Task Intent Throughout Long-Horizon VLA Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context.

extra.full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context. We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. During execution, anomaly monitoring and local recovery re-establish an intent-consistent execution context through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation after persistent deviation. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real-world PiPER tasks. Relative to matched Global-FT baselines, GR00T success on seen composite RoboCasa365 tasks increases from 14.6%/12.1% to 31.8%/20.4% under ID/OOD evaluation. On VLA-Arena, GTI+$π_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. In the three real-robot task experiments, mean full-task success increases from 21.7% to 59.2%. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support.

title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
summary: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots.

extra.comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation at CoRL 2026
extra.full_text: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $π_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

title: Render the Robot, Generate the World: One Video World Model Across Embodiments
summary: Predicting the consequences of an agent's actions requires modeling both the body's motion and the environment's response. Most video world models attempt to learn both from numerical actions, even though geometry and kinematics already specify the intended motion.

extra.full_text: Predicting the consequences of an agent's actions requires modeling both the body's motion and the environment's response. Most video world models attempt to learn both from numerical actions, even though geometry and kinematics already specify the intended motion. We introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model conditioned on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories. By explicitly providing the intended motion, Doppel can focus on predicting object motion and interaction-driven changes in the environment. Rendered motion also provides a common visual interface across different embodiments and action spaces. To train on robot datasets without camera extrinsics, we recover camera poses and align rendered trajectories with recorded observations. We jointly train a single shared video backbone and conditioning adapter on eight datasets spanning eight robot and human embodiments, from single- and bimanual robot arms to a dexterous humanoid and human hands and bodies, using about 600 hours of video without embodiment labels. Across three robot-arm datasets, Doppel improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation, while predicting more consistent object motion. Training on all eight embodiments (Doppel-8) improves robot predictions over the three-robot model (Doppel-3) on four of six evaluation sets. Project page: https://doppelwm.github.io/.

title: ExecGap: Exploiting Command-Execution Gap for Patch Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation.

extra.full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation. Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities. Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion. Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks. Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.

title: SemPhys: Semantic-Physical Co-Learning for Humanoid Motion Generation via Differentiable World Models
summary: In human-robot collaboration, natural language lets people direct a humanoid's whole-body movements without programming joint trajectories. A common approach generates a kinematic reference from an instruction and relies on a tracking controller to execute it.

extra.full_text: In human-robot collaboration, natural language lets people direct a humanoid's whole-body movements without programming joint trajectories. A common approach generates a kinematic reference from an instruction and relies on a tracking controller to execute it. However, as the controller maintains balance under contact constraints, the executed motion can depart from the reference in ways that change the action it conveys. Our central insight is that semantic alignment must be evaluated directly on the complete motion the robot physically executes. Building on this insight, we introduce \textbf{SemPhys}, a framework that trains motion generators using semantic feedback from simulated executions. A differentiable world model and a fixed tracking controller predict a short segment of a recorded execution. SemPhys inserts this prediction at its original position, scores the complete trajectory against the instruction, and backpropagates through the predicted segment. A paired anchoring loss stabilizes adaptation by keeping each generated reference close to its counterpart from the initial generator. On BONES-SEED, SemPhys largely preserves instruction retrieval accuracy from reference to execution and achieves the highest retrieval accuracy on executed motions among the evaluated methods.

title: TinyARM-X: A Series of Open-Source, Configurable, and Transparent Torque-Controlled Desktop-Scale Robotic Manipulators
summary: Visuomotor policies have demonstrated that imprecise low-cost robots can autonomously complete complex manipulation tasks. However, most inexpensive manipulators rely on compact and rigidly position-controlled servos for actuation, which complicate simulation, operation, and safety.

extra.comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to a robotics Journal. Reviews have not come in yet
extra.full_text: Visuomotor policies have demonstrated that imprecise low-cost robots can autonomously complete complex manipulation tasks. However, most inexpensive manipulators rely on compact and rigidly position-controlled servos for actuation, which complicate simulation, operation, and safety. This work introduces TinyARM-X, a framework for easily manufacturable, configurable, and torque-controllable low-cost (<350 USD) serial manipulators. By using a single hardware/software architecture, a <7 Degree of Freedom (DoF) TinyARM can be manually reconfigured to an operational >3 DoF robot within 10 min. Actuator modeling and dynamic compensation enable torque-controlled applications like mixed-reality impedance control teleoperation and simulator force feedback rendering. Experiments include mechanical benchmarking and real-world force-aware telemanipulation. The TinyARM-7 has a payload of 33.5 g, a max speed of 0.77 m/s, and a reach of 210 mm. Moreover, with dynamic compensation, the robot has a backdrive-breakaway force of 1.4 N and a backdrive-running force of 0.7 N. Additionally, Cartesian-Impedance Control (CIC) attains a translational stiffness of >15 N/m. Lastly, the TinyARM-X stack is open-sourced to disseminate accessible desktop-scale torque-controlled robotic manipulation to the community.

title: Proprioceptive Simultaneous Base and Terrain Elevation Estimation for Legged Robot Locomotion
summary: Legged robots in visually degraded environments must rely exclusively on proprioceptive sensing, under which global position and yaw are unobservable. Vertical drift is particularly detrimental, as it corrupts the height reference required by swing-leg trajectories and can destabilize the robot.

extra.full_text: Legged robots in visually degraded environments must rely exclusively on proprioceptive sensing, under which global position and yaw are unobservable. Vertical drift is particularly detrimental, as it corrupts the height reference required by swing-leg trajectories and can destabilize the robot. We treat the terrain itself as a persistent proprioceptive landmark: every footstep provides a height measurement that anchors the vertical axis. We propose Simultaneous Base and Elevation Estimation (SBEE), a real-time open-source framework in which a Left-Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (LI-EKF) for floating-base estimation and a grid-based elevation map are coupled in a bidirectional loop, mirroring SLAM with terrain elevation in place of landmarks. Stable foot contacts insert uncertainty-aware height samples into the map, and previously mapped cells are fed back as uncertainty-weighted vertical pseudo-measurements that act analogously to loop closures. Unlike contact-aided invariant filters, the LI-EKF consumes a kinematic velocity measurement instead of augmenting the state with a contact model per leg, so its state dimension is independent of the number of legs. We evaluate SBEE in MuJoCo on quadrupedal and bipedal platforms and on the ANYmal-D GrandTour dataset over 296 m of locomotion, reducing the absolute trajectory error by 22.1% relative to the best of three state-of-the-art proprioceptive estimators.

title: CommDreamer: Radio-Geometric World Models for Mapless Cellular-Connected UAV Trajectory Planning
summary: Reliable cellular connectivity and collision-free flight are essential for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations in low-altitude urban canyons, where dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, shadow serving base stations, and create strong co-channel interference at street intersections.

extra.full_text: Reliable cellular connectivity and collision-free flight are essential for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations in low-altitude urban canyons, where dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, shadow serving base stations, and create strong co-channel interference at street intersections. Existing planners either require prior 3D city meshes and channel knowledge maps unavailable onboard, or rely on model-free reinforcement learning with low sample efficiency and poor cross-city generalization. We propose CommDreamer, a mapless radio-geometric world model that fuses raw onboard 3D LiDAR scans, multicell cellular reports, and shift-invariant relative kinematics to jointly infer local obstacle clearance and directional signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) dynamics. Using a categorical recurrent state-space model, CommDreamer compresses multimodal measurement histories into a coordinate-invariant latent belief, enabling the UAV to foresee deep shadow zones and train a lightweight online policy purely via multi-step latent imagination without prior maps or antenna patterns. Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies in our open-source ray-tracing simulator, AeroCity-RT, show that CommDreamer converges within 150 episodes where model-free reinforcement learning fails to complete flights, achieving 100.0% mission success with zero collisions while lifting median route SINR to 8.02 dB and cutting effective SINR outage by over 50% relative to radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines.

title: ReLoco: Unified Humanoid Locomotion and Fall Recovery via Behavior-Conditioned Motion Priors
summary: Humanoid robots must recover from falls and resume commanded motion to sustain locomotion. Learning these behaviors in one policy requires supervision that accommodates both upright movement and ground-contact recovery.

extra.full_text: Humanoid robots must recover from falls and resume commanded motion to sustain locomotion. Learning these behaviors in one policy requires supervision that accommodates both upright movement and ground-contact recovery. We present ReLoco, a framework that uses behavior-conditioned adversarial motion priors to learn locomotion, get-up from arbitrary fallen postures, and command resumption within one proprioceptive policy. During training, robot posture selects the expert pool and conditions a shared discriminator with two behavior-specific outputs. Task rewards and shared regularization support command tracking and recovery, while temporary assistance facilitates exploration. A simulation-based refinement stage supplies robot-executed motion references for this supervision. Ablations examine conditional supervision, output separation, and reference quality under matched settings. At a common training iteration, the full policy achieves $96.80\%$ independent get-up success and $96.96\%$ push-recovery success, including command resumption. Its torso planar velocity root-mean-square error is $0.1266$~m/s, $14.7\%$ lower than the conditional single-output variant, with similar joint-angle discrepancy measured by dynamic time warping. Deployment on the 64.5-kg Tiangong~3.0 humanoid demonstrates walking, running, get-up, and locomotion resumption after falls using one proprioceptive actor, without controller switching or on-robot policy fine-tuning.

title: NereidVLA: Learning to Understand and Navigate the Underwater World
summary: Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation.

extra.full_text: Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation. We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision. We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics. Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.

title: Constructive Infinitely Differentiable Guidance Vector Fields for Robotic Control
summary: Guidance vector fields (GVFs) are a popular framework for tasks such as robotic path-following and multi-robot motion coordination, but existing approaches may be non-differentiable or have large derivatives, limiting their use in controllers that require derivatives of the guidance signal, which is common when the GVF is used as an input in a cascaded controller.

extra.full_text: Guidance vector fields (GVFs) are a popular framework for tasks such as robotic path-following and multi-robot motion coordination, but existing approaches may be non-differentiable or have large derivatives, limiting their use in controllers that require derivatives of the guidance signal, which is common when the GVF is used as an input in a cascaded controller. This paper proposes an infinitely differentiable constructive GVF. The resulting vector field depends on a smoothing parameter and is a generalization of [1], recovering the original GVF in the limit as this parameter approaches zero. It also admits a simple and efficient implementation that preserves smoothness under discretization and can reduce computation time by using substantially fewer curve samples while maintaining small path-following errors. We establish the main theoretical properties and demonstrate its practical advantages through numerical and real-world experiments.

title: QDD-MM: A Simple and Compact Open-Source Muscle Module with Quasi-Direct-Drive Motor for Tendon-driven Robots
summary: Tendon-driven robots, which actuate like biological muscles by using motors to wind wires, offer advantages such as variable stiffness and redundant actuation.

extra.comment: Accepted to IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026, website - https://haraduka.github.io/qddmm/, youtube - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=09xRhZO497k
extra.full_text: Tendon-driven robots, which actuate like biological muscles by using motors to wind wires, offer advantages such as variable stiffness and redundant actuation. Despite these advantages, musculoskeletal structures inherently involve a large number of diverse muscles, making it desirable to compactly modularize each muscle unit and flexibly accommodate diverse muscle arrangements. While various small muscle modules have been proposed to date, existing designs tend to be complex, difficult to maintain, and suffer from low backdrivability and limited actuation speed due to their high gear ratios. In this work, we propose QDD-MM, a muscle module that leverages recent advances in quasi-direct-drive motors to achieve a simpler and more compact structure with higher backdrivability and faster actuation than previous modules. By utilizing quasi-direct-drive motors, the module eliminates the need for dedicated force-sensing mechanisms, significantly simplifying the overall design, while also supporting flexible wire routing in multiple directions, various module-to-module connections, and even the use of the module body itself as a structural component. QDD-MM integrates these capabilities into a reusable muscle module, and its design is openly available at https://github.com/haraduka/qddmm. We developed tendon-driven robots with one joint and either two or three muscles, as well as a partial musculoskeletal humanoid, using the proposed QDD-MM and verified their effectiveness. We expect that this muscle module will democratize tendon-driven robotics and further accelerate progress in the field.

title: Allocentric Memory, Egocentric Acting: A Dual-Frame VLA for Urban Aerial Navigation
summary: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation.

extra.full_text: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.

title: JEPA Dots: Dual-Latent World Model for Language-Guided Robot Control
summary: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations.

extra.full_text: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations. To address this challenge, we introduce JEPA Dots (Dynamics-Oriented Task Separation), a compact dual-latent framework that jointly learns visual dynamics and language-guided control through separate dynamics and task representations. Language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention restricts world prediction to instruction-independent dynamics history and supplied actions. In closed-loop evaluation on 40 trained LIBERO tasks, JEPA Dots achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters, compared with the published 78.7% of NanoVLA-S with 161.0M parameters under a different evaluation protocol. In the reference experiment, JEPA Dots also improves overall success from 76.0% for our task-ID-conditioned adaptation baseline to 84.9%, with LIBERO-Goal success increasing from 67.1% to 88.5%. Instruction-switching experiments further confirm that task representations and policy outputs respond to language changes, while dynamics representations and world predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and supplied actions.

title: RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling.

extra.full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling.   In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view.   We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73.   Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $π_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.

title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
summary: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

extra.full_text: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change. For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “ Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On .”

summary: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? extra.full_text: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. summary: 3D affordance acts as a critical link between perception and action, providing priors for robotic manipulation. While existing approaches predominantly leverage human priors as direct references, they often overlook that affordance is not an object-intrinsic property but is inherently coupled with the agent's embodiment.

extra.full_text: 3D affordance acts as a critical link between perception and action, providing priors for robotic manipulation. While existing approaches predominantly leverage human priors as direct references, they often overlook that affordance is not an object-intrinsic property but is inherently coupled with the agent's embodiment. Due to the structural and morphological disparities between human hands and robot end-effectors, directly applying human priors causes severe incompatibility for robotic execution. Motivated by this, we introduce a novel task setting, 3D Human-to-Robot Affordance Transfer, which addresses the affordance misalignment arising from distinct embodiment structures. To support this task, we construct the Human-Robot Paired Affordance Dataset (HPAD), the first large-scale 3D affordance benchmark in which every object is annotated with both human-prior and simulation-validated robot labels. HPAD covers 2,137 objects across 80 categories and 13 atomic action primitives, yielding over 27,000 object-action pairs. On top of HPAD, we propose the 3D Affordance tRansfer neTwork (ART). ART first filters geometric false positives in the human prior via a reliability gating stream, then reconstructs the prior into a robot-actionable distribution through hierarchical reconstruction and a graph-diffusion refinement that resolves the topological mismatch between human and robot affordances. Experiments on HPAD demonstrate the reliability of the proposed task and the superiority of ART. We further validate ART on a 6-DoF arm with a parallel-jaw gripper in a 2,400-execution benchmark across 12 objects and 4 action categories; ART attains the best success rate (86.5% over its 480 trials), confirming the practicality of the transfer paradigm. title: AeroRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight.

extra.comment: 8-page main paper with references and supplementary material (15 pages); 5 figures, 13 tables. Code: https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI Project page: https://starsholic.github.io/AeroRSI/
extra.full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.

title: Phoenix: Learning Scene Structure Representations for Generalizable World-Action Models
summary: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling.

extra.full_text: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.

title: Estimation-Aware Reachability
summary: Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability computes the states from which a system can be kept safe under worst-case disturbances, but it assumes the state is known exactly, whereas real robots act on noisy estimates whose uncertainty evolves with their motion.

extra.full_text: Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability computes the states from which a system can be kept safe under worst-case disturbances, but it assumes the state is known exactly, whereas real robots act on noisy estimates whose uncertainty evolves with their motion. We extend Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability to the robot's belief, estimate and uncertainty, treating unexpected measurements as a bounded adversary and enlarging the unsafe set by the current uncertainty, so that certified states are safe with a prescribed probability. The formulation is compatible with existing solvers. In simulation, the resulting safety filters nearly eliminate the collisions of certaintyequivalent HJ and are less conservative than equally safe uncertainty-padding baselines. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/HimanshuPaudel/Estimation-Aware-Reachability

title: DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings
summary: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing.

extra.full_text: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. We formalize these metrics in a unified integral form and show that the weight of a local error decays as the $(k+q)$-th power of its size, where $k$ is the dimension of the integration domain and $q$ is determined by the penalty function. Guided by this analysis, we propose DrawScore, which projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines, as in engineering drawings, and applies a saturating penalty along the projected curves, so that the weight of a local error decays only linearly. Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders, and on outputs of existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs that IoU rates as nearly perfect. DrawScore further improves generation as a reinforcement learning reward and, for CAD generation from engineering drawings, serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth or an additional reward model. Our code is available at https://github.com/UESTC-Simon/DrawScore.

title: Asymmetric Decomposition for Multi-Agent Path Finding with Unassigned Agents
summary: Robots without assigned tasks may obstruct active robots, while routing them to designated parking locations can cause unnecessary travel. This article proposes flow-oracle conflict-based search (FOCBS) for Multi-Agent Path Finding with unassigned agents (MAPF-UA).

extra.full_text: Robots without assigned tasks may obstruct active robots, while routing them to designated parking locations can cause unnecessary travel. This article proposes flow-oracle conflict-based search (FOCBS) for Multi-Agent Path Finding with unassigned agents (MAPF-UA). FOCBS searches over assigned-agent paths using conflict-based search (CBS) and routes targetless unassigned agents through a min-cost flow oracle. When the selected assigned-agent paths leave unassigned agents no collision-free paths, flow-conflict branching converts min-cut blockers into assigned-agent constraints, which guide the search without excluding optimal solutions. A batched zero-cost warm start accelerates the oracle, and start-avoiding tie-breaking reduces unassigned-agent movement. For feasible instances on finite graphs, we prove termination and global minimization of assigned-agent sum of service time, measured by last-arrival times. Unassigned-agent movement is minimized conditional on the selected assigned-agent paths, without a global lexicographic optimality guarantee. Benchmark experiments show that FOCBS scales well with the number of unassigned agents, and ablation studies show that, compared with discarding non-completable assigned-agent paths, flow-conflict branching solves substantially more instances while retaining optimality. Simulation and physical-robot experiments demonstrate plan executability, with laboratory tests reducing fleet travel by 40.8% relative to the parking-based coordination baseline. The source code and related resources are available at https://github.com/Chin-hsi/focbs

title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
summary: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed.

extra.full_text: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell , the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die . The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies , the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke. “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics , based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death. When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away. Christie Hemm Klok The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.” For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold. But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga , who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit. Why Telesurgery Starts With Stroke As recently as the early ’90s , physicians who treated stroke struggled with “ therapeutic nihilism .” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery . In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event. Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right. The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.” Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter. Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray. I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction. This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says. About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.” Telesurgery’s Second Act Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications. But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries . In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform. Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “ telecollaboration ,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery ; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet. “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations. Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage. Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain— steered with magnets to dissolve a clot. When Surgery Depends on the Network After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity. In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds . In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100. Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations , they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says. Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot. But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.” Where Telesurgery Could Work Best During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure. Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy center s serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range. But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu , an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it. Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System. Remedy Robotics And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says. Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.” –neurologist Archit Bhatt Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra , an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission. “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.” Measures of Success If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent. In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster. Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept. The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels— were a success , and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people. In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027. Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.” The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery. These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.
